# Introduction to Jeremiah

## Part 1: General Introduction

### Outline of the Book of Jeremiah

1. Yahweh calls Jeremiah to be a prophet (1:1–19))
2. Yahweh will judge and punish Judah (2:1–29:32)
    * Judah called to repent of spiritual adultery (2:1–6:30)
    * Judah judged for its false religion (7:1–10:16)
    * Jeremiah stands between Yahweh and his people (11:1–20:19)
    * Jeremiah confronts his people (21:1–29:32)
3. Yahweh promises to restore Judah (30:1–33:26)
    * Yahweh will bring the people of Judah back to their land (30:1–24)
    * Yahweh will create a new covenant with them (31:1–40)
    * The people will come back (32:1–44)
    * Kings descended from David will rule again (33:1–26)
4. Jeremiah suffers (34:1–45:5)
    * Before Yahweh punishes Judah (34:1–36:32)
    * While Yahweh punishes Judah (37:1–39:18)
    * After Yahweh punishes Judah (40:1–45:5)
5. Yahweh will judge and punish the nations (46:1–51:64)
    * Egypt (46:1–28)
    * Philistia (47:1–28)
    * Moab (48:1–47)
    * Ammon (49:1–6)
    * Edom (49:7–22)
    * Damascus (49:23–27)
    * Kedar (49:28–33)
    * Elam (49:34–39)
    * Babylonia (50:1–51:64)
6. Jerusalem captured and destroyed (52:1–34)

### What is the Book of Jeremiah about?

The Book of Jeremiah gives the prophesies of a priest named Jeremiah. It also tells how Jeremiah suffered in different ways while he prophesied.

Jeremiah began prophesying about 626 B.C. After the death of King Josiah, many groups of people in Israel opposed Jeremiah. Some of these people wanted to depend on Egypt to protect the nation. Others were idol worshipers. They hated Jeremiah for denouncing their gods.

During the reign of King Jehoiakim, Jeremiah prophesied about the temple of Yahweh. King Jehoiakim received some of these prophecies in writing and burned the document. The next king, Zedekiah, put Jeremiah in prison when he told the king to surrender to Babylon.

King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylonia invaded Judah in 597 B.C. He conquered Jerusalem in 587 B.C. He offered Jeremiah housing and money if Jeremiah would go to Babylon. But Jeremiah remained in Jerusalem to help the few Jews left there.

Shortly after that, Gedaliah, whom Nebuchadnezzar had chosen to be governor over Judah, was murdered. Some Jewish rebels captured Jeremiah and took him to Egypt. Those rebels went to Egypt to be protected there rather than to live under Nebuchadnezzar’s rule. Jeremiah may have died soon after being taken to Egypt. But while in Egypt he prophesied that the Babylonians would invade and conquer Egypt.

### How should the title of this book be translated?

The traditional title of this book is “The Book of Jeremiah” or just “Jeremiah.” Translators may also call it the “The Book about Jeremiah” or “What the Prophet Jeremiah Said.”

### Who wrote the Book of Jeremiah?

Jeremiah was a priest and a prophet living in Judah. He spoke the prophesies in the Book of Jeremiah. A friend named Baruch wrote down many of the prophecies as Jeremiah spoke them to him.

## Part 2: Important Religious and Cultural Concepts

### What is the new covenant that is presented in the Book of Jeremiah?

Jeremiah introduced a “new covenant” between Yahweh and Israel (chapter 31). Yahweh would “write this covenant on the hearts” of the people. This means that the covenant would be a part of the people instead of just written on stone or paper. The people would obey the new covenant with all their heart.

### What relationship do Jeremiah’s prophecies have to the other nations besides Israel?

Much of the Old Testament before this time is only about the nation of Israel. But Jeremiah also spoke of how Yahweh would judge other nations of the world. Yahweh would also punish the other nations for their wicked deeds.

## Part 3: Important Translation Issues

### Are the events in the Book of Jeremiah told in the order that they actually happened?

Many of the events in the Book of Jeremiah are not told in the order that they actually happened. Instead, the various prophecies appear to be arranged by topic.

### Why does the Book of Jeremiah refer to this prophet as “he” or “him”?

Many times in the book, the author refers to Jeremiah as “Jeremiah” or “he.” This is unusual if Jeremiah wrote the book. The reason this occurs is perhaps because Baruch, Jeremiah’s secretary, wrote down some parts of the book. Translators should keep the words “Jeremiah” and “he.”

# Jeremiah 1 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

The chapter moves from a dated heading (1:1–3) to Jeremiah’s call (1:4–10), two visions (1:11–16), and Yahweh’s charge (1:17–19). The ULT formats 1:5 and 1:7–8 as poetry.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Commissioning a prophet

Yahweh set Jeremiah apart before birth and put his words in Jeremiah’s mouth. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet]])

# Jeremiah 2 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This is a covenant lawsuit in poetry. Yahweh recalls Israel’s early devotion (2:1–3), indicts the nation for abandoning him (2:4–19), and exposes its unfaithfulness (2:20–37).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Israel as an unfaithful wife

Yahweh pictures the covenant as a marriage, so idolatry appears as prostitution. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/prostitute]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Rhetorical questions

Yahweh accuses mainly through rhetorical questions, and paired lines often restate one idea.

Jeremiah is using **the word of Yahweh was to me** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Yahweh gave me a message.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh spoke a message to me, saying]

Jeremiah is using the words translated as **And the word of Yahweh was to me** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

Quote: הָלֹ֡ךְ וְ⁠קָֽרָאתָ֩ בְ⁠אָזְנֵ֨י יְרוּשָׁלִַ֜ם לֵ⁠אמֹ֗ר כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה
Note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Go and proclaim in the ears of Jerusalem that I, Yahweh, say this]

The word **you** is singular here because Yahweh is addressing the city of Jerusalem as though she were one woman, so use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how you were faithful to my covenant when you were young]

Yahweh is speaking as if the early days of the nation of Israel were a person’s **youth**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the covenant faithfulness of your early days as a nation]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **love**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how you loved me in the early days of our relationship]

Yahweh is speaking as if the beginning of his covenant relationship with Israel were the time of **your betrothal**, when a man and a woman were promised to each other before their marriage. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. # Jeremiah 3 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Poetry and prose alternate: there is an appeal to unfaithful Judah (3:1–5), a contrast of apostate Israel and treacherous Judah (3:6–11), a call to return (3:12–18), and a closing confession (3:19–25).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The law about divorce

Verse 1 assumes the existence of the law forbidding a remarried woman to return to her first husband (see [Deuteronomy 24:1-4](../deu/24/01.md)). Yahweh applies it to Israel and Judah as adulterous wives. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/adultery]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

Yahweh, the prophet, and the people all speak, and the changes are unmarked.
The term **Saying** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

# Jeremiah 4 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter moves from a call for Israel to return to Yahweh (4:1–4) to poetic alarm over an invading army from the north (4:5–31).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Circumcision of the heart

In [4:4](../04/04.md), circumcision, the covenant sign, is an image of inward devotion. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/circumcise]])

### Jeremiah’s accusation that Yahweh deceived the people

In [4:10](../04/10.md), Jeremiah says to Yahweh, “Ah, Lord Yahweh, surely deceiving, you have deceived this people and Jerusalem, saying, ‘It will be peace for you.’ Yet the sword will reach as far as the life.” Here Jeremiah is not stating the Yahweh himself promised the people of Judah “peace.” Rather, he is saying that it was the false prophets who deceived the people. Jeremiah is expressing his frustration that the people of Judah are about to be slaughtered. He knows Yahweh is sovereign and could have stopped this from happening, so he is expressing his complaint to Yahweh because he knows that Yahweh is ultimately responsible for allowing the people of Judah to be deceived by the deceptive messages of the false prophets.

# Jeremiah 5 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is mostly poetry about a search through Jerusalem for one just person (5:1–9), a warning of an invading nation (5:10–19), and an indictment of a people who will not fear Yahweh (5:20–31).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Lying prophets

The prophets speak falsely, the priests rule by their own authority, and the people approve. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

Speakers change without announcement, and the people’s words are quoted inside Yahweh’s speech.

# Jeremiah 6 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter comprised poetry throughout: alarm to flee the army from the north (6:1–8), Yahweh’s verdict on people who will not listen (6:9–21), terror as the army advances (6:22–26), and Jeremiah as a tester of metal (6:27–30).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Uncircumcised ear

In [6:10](../06/10.md), the covenant sign becomes an image for ears that will not hear Yahweh. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/circumcise]])

# Jeremiah 7 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh commands Jeremiah to preach at the gate of the temple, calling Judah to amend its conduct and warning that the sanctuary will not protect Judah.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Trust in the temple

The people assumed the [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/temple]] guaranteed their safety; Yahweh cites [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/names/shiloh]], a sanctuary he destroyed.

# Jeremiah 8 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Yahweh’s judgment speech from chapter 7, moving from desecrated graves (verses 1–3), to the refusal to repent (verses 4–13), to invasion and lament (verses 14–22).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The host of the heavens

The people worshiped the sun, moon, and stars as gods. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/falsegod]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Unmarked speaker changes

The speaker shifts among Yahweh, the people, and the prophet without introduction, notably at verses 14, 18, and 19.

Jeremiah is using **the declaration of Yahweh** to indicate that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

# Jeremiah 9 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is mostly poetry, moving from Jeremiah’s lament over his people’s deceit to Yahweh’s sentence of refining, desolation, and exile.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Circumcision of the heart

Verses 25–26 contrast bodily circumcision with the inward loyalty to Yahweh that Israel lacks.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

# Jeremiah 10 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter contrasts the worthless idols of the nations with Yahweh, the living God and creator (verses 1–16), then announces the coming exile and Jeremiah’s lament (verses 17–25).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Making idols

Verses 3–5, 9, and 14 describe craftsmen shaping false gods from wood and overlaying them with silver and gold.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Changes of speaker

The chapter shifts speakers without warning between Yahweh, Jeremiah, and the personified city.

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the descendants of Jacob were a **house**, that is, a single family living together. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people of the nation of Israel]

The word translated as **for** indicates how this statement relates to the command that comes before it. This could mean: (1) that it gives the reason why the people of Israel should not be dismayed, since fearing these signs is what the nations do or (2) that it concedes that the nations are indeed dismayed by these signs, even though the people of Israel should not be. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. # Jeremiah 11 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh sends Jeremiah to proclaim the covenant and its curses to Judah (verses 1-17); Jeremiah then laments a plot against his life (verses 18-23).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Covenant curses

Judah broke the covenant Yahweh made at the exodus and built altars to Baal, so its curses now fall as disaster.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

Yahweh’s messages nest speech several layers deep. Consider marking the levels clearly or making inner quotations indirect.

# Jeremiah 12 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Verses 1-13 are poetry. Jeremiah complains that wicked people prosper (verses 1-4); Yahweh answers (verses 5-6), laments abandoning his people (verses 7-13), and promises to uproot and restore Judah’s neighbors (verses 14-17).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Yahweh’s inheritance

Yahweh calls his people his house, his inheritance, and his vineyard.

# Jeremiah 13 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Prose sign acts—the ruined linen loincloth (verses 1–11) and the wine jars (verses 12–14)—give way to poetry announcing exile for Judah’s pride (verses 15–27).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Prophetic sign acts

Yahweh had Jeremiah perform symbolic actions and then explained them as pictures of Judah’s ruin and coming [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/exile]].

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations within quotations

Verses 12–14 nest quotations several levels deep; some languages may need indirect speech.
See how you translated the similar expression in [2:5](../02/05.md). This also occurs in verses 9, 12, and 13 of this chapter.

Quote: הָל֞וֹךְ וְ⁠קָנִ֤יתָ לְּ⁠ךָ֙ אֵז֣וֹר פִּשְׁתִּ֔ים וְ⁠שַׂמְתּ֖⁠וֹ עַל־מָתְנֶ֑י⁠ךָ
Note: Buying a linen loincloth and putting it around his waist was a symbolic action by which Jeremiah showed how closely Yahweh had bound the people of Israel and Judah to himself. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Go and buy a linen loincloth for yourself and put it around your loins, to show how closely I have bound my people to myself]

A **linen loincloth** is a kind of undergarment made of cloth that a man wrapped around his waist and hips. If your readers would not be familiar with what a linen loincloth is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [a cloth undergarment made of linen]

The implication is that Yahweh is telling Jeremiah not to wash the loincloth. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [but do not let it get wet by washing it]
See how you translated this expression in [8:9](../08/09.md). This also occurs in verses 3 and 8 of this chapter.

Jeremiah is using **And the word of Yahweh was to me a second time** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Yahweh spoke to me again.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh spoke to me again]
See how you translated the similar expression in [1:4](../01/04.md).

Yahweh is using **arise** as a common expression of the culture to mean “set out to do something.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and set out and go to Perath]
The word **Perath** is the name of a place. This also occurs in verses 5–7.

Jeremiah is using the phrase translated as **And it happened from the end of many days** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

Jeremiah is using **from the end of many days** as a common expression of the culture to mean “after a long time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [after a long time had passed]

Jeremiah is using the term **behold** to focus his readers’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and look]

The expression **was ruined** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the loincloth had rotted away]
See how you translated the similar expression in [1:4](../01/04.md).

Quote: כֹּ֖ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֑ה כָּ֠כָה אַשְׁחִ֞ית אֶת־גְּא֧וֹן יְהוּדָ֛ה
Note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that in this way he will ruin the majesty of Judah]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **majesty**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what makes Judah majestic and what makes Jerusalem so very majestic]

Here, **Judah** and **Jerusalem** represent “the people who live in those places.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the majesty of the people of Judah and the great majesty of the people living in Jerusalem]

Quote: הָ⁠עָם֩ הַ⁠זֶּ֨ה הָ⁠רָ֜ע הַֽ⁠מֵּאֲנִ֣ים לִ⁠שְׁמ֣וֹעַ אֶת־דְּבָרַ֗⁠י הַ⁠הֹֽלְכִים֙ בִּ⁠שְׁרִר֣וּת לִבָּ֔⁠ם וַ⁠יֵּלְכ֗וּ אַֽחֲרֵי֙ אֱלֹהִ֣ים אֲחֵרִ֔ים לְ⁠עָבְדָ֖⁠ם וּ⁠לְ⁠הִשְׁתַּחֲוֺ֣ת לָ⁠הֶ֑ם וִ⁠יהִי֙ כָּ⁠אֵז֣וֹר הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה
Note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about what Yahweh will do to these people before the long description of who they are and what they have done. Alternate translation: [I will punish this evil people—the ones who refuse to listen to my words, the ones walking in the stubbornness of their heart, and they have walked after other gods to serve them and to bow down to them. Let them be like this loincloth]

Quote: הָ⁠עָם֩ הַ⁠זֶּ֨ה הָ⁠רָ֜ע הַֽ⁠מֵּאֲנִ֣ים לִ⁠שְׁמ֣וֹעַ אֶת־דְּבָרַ֗⁠י הַ⁠הֹֽלְכִים֙ בִּ⁠שְׁרִר֣וּת לִבָּ֔⁠ם וַ⁠יֵּלְכ֗וּ אַֽחֲרֵי֙ אֱלֹהִ֣ים אֲחֵרִ֔ים לְ⁠עָבְדָ֖⁠ם וּ⁠לְ⁠הִשְׁתַּחֲוֺ֣ת לָ⁠הֶ֑ם וִ⁠יהִי֙ כָּ⁠אֵז֣וֹר הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה
Note: In this verse, the word **people** is singular in form, but it refers to all of the people of Judah as a group, and Yahweh refers back to it with the singular pronoun **him**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “people” and a plural pronoun. Alternate translation: [These evil people … let them be like this loincloth]

The implication is that these people refuse to obey what Yahweh tells them, not merely that they refuse to hear it. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the ones who refuse to obey my words]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the way these people live were **walking**, and as if what they are determined to do were the **stubbornness of their heart**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones living according to their own stubborn desires]
See how you translated this expression in [9:14](../09/14.md).

Here Yahweh is speaking as if these people had **walked after other gods** when they served them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they have followed other gods]

Bowing down before an image was a symbolic action by which a person showed that he worshiped the god that the image represented. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and to bow down before their images to worship them]

Quote: וִ⁠יהִי֙ כָּ⁠אֵז֣וֹר הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר לֹא־יִצְלַ֖ח לַ⁠כֹּֽל
Note: The point of this comparison is that just as **this loincloth** is **not good for anything**, so these people will be of no use to Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [let him become useless to me, just as this loincloth is not good for anything]

Quote: כִּ֡י כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁר֩ יִדְבַּ֨ק הָ⁠אֵז֜וֹר אֶל־מָתְנֵי־אִ֗ישׁ כֵּ֣ן הִדְבַּ֣קְתִּי אֵ֠לַ⁠י אֶת־כָּל־בֵּ֨ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֜ל וְ⁠אֶת־כָּל־בֵּ֤ית יְהוּדָה֙
Note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a loincloth clings to the loins of a man**, so Yahweh bound the people of Israel and Judah closely to himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [For just as a loincloth stays tightly wrapped around a man’s waist, so I bound the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah closely to myself]

Yahweh is not referring to a specific **man**. He means men in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the loins of men]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if all the descendants of Israel and of Judah were a **house**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all the descendants of Israel and all the descendants of Judah]
See how you translated the similar expression in [1:8](../01/08.md). This also occurs in verses 14 and 25.

The terms **name**, **praise**, and **glory** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the three terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [and be for my great renown]
Here, **name** represents renown. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and be for renown]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **praise** and **glory**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [and to praise me, and to honor me as glorious]

The word translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [Because of that, you shall speak]

Quote: כֹּֽה־אָמַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל כָּל־נֵ֖בֶל יִמָּ֣לֵא יָ֑יִן
Note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [that Yahweh, the God of Israel, says that every jar shall be filled with wine]

The expression **shall be filled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [You must fill every jar with wine]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people of Judah were jars that he would fill with **wine**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Every one of you will be filled with wine like a jar]

A **jar** is a kind of large clay container that people used for storing wine. If your readers would not be familiar with what a jar is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [Every large container for liquid]

Quote: הֲ⁠יָדֹ֨עַ֙ לֹ֣א נֵדַ֔ע כִּ֥י כָל־נֵ֖בֶל יִמָּ֥לֵא יָֽיִן
Note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [that they know very well that every jar will be filled with wine]

Quote: הֲ⁠יָדֹ֨עַ֙ לֹ֣א נֵדַ֔ע כִּ֥י כָל־נֵ֖בֶל יִמָּ֥לֵא יָֽיִן
Note: The people are using the question form to express scorn for what Jeremiah has told them. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [We certainly know that every jar will be filled with wine!]

The people are repeating forms of the verb **know** in order to intensify their expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Do we not know with certainty]

The expression **will be filled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people fill every jar with wine]
The pronoun **they** refers to the people of Judah and Jerusalem. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the people will say to you, Jeremiah]

Quote: כֹּֽה־אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה הִנְ⁠נִ֣י מְמַלֵּ֣א & וְ⁠אֶת & שִׁכָּרֽוֹן
Note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that he will fill with drunkenness]

Yahweh is using **Behold** with the participle that follows as a common expression of the culture to mean “I am about to do this.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am about to fill]

Quote: כֹּֽה־אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה הִנְ⁠נִ֣י מְמַלֵּ֣א אֶת־כָּל־יֹשְׁבֵ֣י הָ⁠אָ֪רֶץ הַ⁠זֹּ֟את & שִׁכָּרֽוֹן
Note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the helplessness that he will bring on the people of this land were **drunkenness** with which he would fill them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says, “I am about to make all of the ones inhabiting this land completely helpless]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **drunkenness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with the appearance that they are drunk]

Here, **throne** represents royal authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the ones exercising royal authority]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people were jars that he would **smash** against one another. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will destroy each man along with his brother]
See how you translated this expression in [6:21](../06/21.md).

The terms **pity**, **spare**, and **have compassion** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the three terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [I will show them no mercy at all]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative expression **so as not to destroy them**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [and I will have no compassion, but I will surely destroy them] or [and I will have no compassion that would cause me to preserve them]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **compassion**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and I will not act compassionately]

The verbs **Listen**, **give ear**, and **be proud** are plural here because Jeremiah is addressing the people of Judah, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The terms **Listen** and **give ear** mean similar things. Jeremiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Listen very carefully]
Here, **ear** represents “paying attention.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and pay attention]

Jeremiah is using **Give glory to Yahweh your God** as a common expression of the culture to mean “honor Yahweh your God.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Show honor to Yahweh your God]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the disaster that Yahweh will bring on the people were **darkness**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [before he brings a time of disaster]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the ruin that will come on the people were their **feet** stumbling on mountain paths in the dark. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he brings ruin on you while you are helpless in the growing dark]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the deliverance that the people hope for were **light**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you hope for deliverance]

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [but he turns it into utterly gloomy darkness]

Jeremiah is presenting a possible condition, that the people of Judah will refuse to listen to what Yahweh says. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [But suppose you refuse to listen. Then my soul will weep in secret places]
Here, **my soul** represents “I myself.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I myself will weep]

Jeremiah is using **in secret places** as a common expression of the culture to mean “where no one else can see.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [where no one can see me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **pride**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your proud behavior]
The pronoun **she** refers to the soul of Jeremiah, which he mentions earlier in the verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and my soul will weep bitterly]

Jeremiah is repeating forms of the verb **weep** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [and she will weep bitterly]

The expression **has been taken captive** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [enemies have taken Yahweh’s flock captive]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the people of Judah were a **flock** of sheep that belongs to Yahweh. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s people have been taken captive]

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Tell the king and to the queen mother to make themselves low, sit down]

If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Come down from your thrones and sit on the ground to show that you are humbled and mourning]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **the crown of your glory** before the information about what has happened to it. Alternate translation: [for the crown of your glory has come down from your heads]
Here, **crown** represents royal authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your glorious royal authority]

The implication is that enemy armies will besiege these cities so that no one can go in or out of them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [The cities of the Negev are shut up by besieging armies, and no one can pass in or out of them]

The expression **are shut up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Enemies have shut up the cities of the Negev]

The expressions **has been exiled** and **has been wholly exiled** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Enemies have carried away all of Judah, they have carried her away completely]

In this verse, the word **Judah** is singular in form, and Yahweh refers back to it with the singular pronoun **she**, but it refers to all of the people of Judah as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “Judah” and a plural pronoun. Alternate translation: [have been exiled, they have been wholly exiled]
The word **your** is plural here because Yahweh is addressing the people of Jerusalem, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Yahweh is using **Lift up your eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean “look.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Look and see]

The implication is that **the ones coming from the north** are enemy armies that will invade the land. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the invading armies that are coming from the north]

Yahweh is using the question form to rebuke the leaders of Jerusalem for failing to care for the people whom he entrusted to them. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You have lost the flock given to you, your beautiful flock!]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people of Judah were a **flock** of sheep that he had entrusted to their leaders. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people entrusted to you, your beautiful people]

The expression **given to you** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the flock that God gave to you]

Quote: מַה־תֹּֽאמְרִי֙ כִּֽי־יִפְקֹ֣ד עָלַ֔יִ⁠ךְ וְ֠⁠אַתְּ לִמַּ֨דְתְּ אֹתָ֥⁠ם עָלַ֛יִ⁠ךְ אַלֻּפִ֖ים לְ⁠רֹ֑אשׁ
Note: Yahweh is using the question form to warn the people of Judah about what is going to happen to them. Quote: עָלַ֔יִ⁠ךְ וְ֠⁠אַתְּ לִמַּ֨דְתְּ אֹתָ֥⁠ם עָלַ֛יִ⁠ךְ אַלֻּפִ֖ים לְ⁠רֹ֑אשׁ
Note: The implication is that the nations whom the people of Judah had cultivated as allies will become the rulers over them. Here, **head** represents “ruler.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to be ruler]

Quote: הֲ⁠ל֤וֹא חֲבָלִים֙ יֹאחֱז֔וּ⁠ךְ כְּמ֖וֹ אֵ֥שֶׁת לֵדָֽה
Note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that great anguish will certainly come upon the people of Judah. Alternate translation: [Surely labor pains will seize you like a woman in labor!]

If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [suddenly and severely, causing you great anguish]

Yahweh is using **say in your heart** as a common expression of the culture to mean “think to yourself.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And if you ask yourself]

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And when you ask yourself why these things have come upon you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Because you have sinned so much]

If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [your enemies have uncovered your skirts and exposed your heels]

Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [your women have been stripped naked and raped]
Alternate translation: [When]

If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [No Cushite can change the color of his skin, and no leopard can change its spots!]
The word **Cushite** is the name of a people group.

Alternate translation: [Then, in the same way, you yourself are not able to do good, because you are accustomed to do evil]

Yahweh is using the adjective **accustomed** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [you who are used to doing evil]

# Jeremiah 14 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh, Jeremiah, and the people speak in turn about a drought, false prophets, and judgment. Verses 7-9 and 19-22 are communal laments.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Drought as judgment

Withheld rain signaled judgment on covenant unfaithfulness; the dry wells of verses 2-6 mark Judah’s guilt.

The speaker changes without introduction at verses 7, 13, and 19, so translators may need to name each speaker.

# Jeremiah 15 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

The chapter moves from Yahweh’s refusal to spare Judah (verses 1–9) to Jeremiah’s lament and Yahweh’s answer to him (verses 10–21). Much of it is poetry.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Intercession

Moses and Samuel were remembered as men whose prayers turned Yahweh’s anger aside. Not even their intercession would spare Judah.

# Jeremiah 16 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh forbids Jeremiah to marry, to mourn, or to feast, so his life becomes a sign of coming judgment (verses 1–9); verses 10–21 explain the exile and promise a return.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Mourning customs

Verses 5–8 mention the funeral banquet house, ritual gashing and shaving, and the cup of consolation.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations within quotations

Yahweh’s speech often contains further quotations, and the speaker changes to Jeremiah at verse 19.

# Jeremiah 17 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter gathers several short poetic units that contrast trust in Yahweh with trust in human strength, and it closes with a prose sermon about the Sabbath.

  1. Judah’s engraved sin and the loss of her inheritance (1–4)
  2. Two contrasting portraits of trust (5–8)
    1. Cursed is the man who trusts in mankind, like a shrub in the desert (5–6)
    2. Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, like a tree planted by waters (7–8)
  3. The deceitful heart and Yahweh who searches it (9–11)
  4. Jeremiah’s prayer for healing and for vindication against those who mock him (12–18)
  5. Yahweh’s message about the Sabbath at the gates of Jerusalem (19–27)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in [17:1–18](../17/01.md).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Altars, Asherim, and high places

In verses 2–3 the people worship at altars and Asherah poles beside green trees on the hills rather than at the temple. Yahweh treats this worship as the reason he will hand over Judah’s wealth and the land he gave her. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/names/asherim]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/inherit]])

### Keeping the Sabbath holy

In verses 19–27 the command not to bear a burden on the Sabbath refers to carrying goods for trade or doing ordinary work on that day. Yahweh sets obedience and disobedience before the people as two paths with opposite outcomes. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sabbath]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Changes of speaker

The chapter moves between Yahweh speaking, the prophet speaking about the righteous and the wicked, and Jeremiah praying, often with no statement identifying the new speaker. You may need to make each change of speaker explicit.

### Extended comparisons

The contrast in verses 5–8 is developed through two sustained images, a shrub in a salt desert and a tree planted beside water, with a further comparison in verse 11. If your readers would not understand these images, it may help to state the point of each comparison alongside it.

# Jeremiah 18 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh sends Jeremiah to watch a potter at work and then explains what that scene means for Israel, for any nation, and for Judah in particular. The chapter ends with a plot against Jeremiah and his prayer against the men who made it.

  1. Yahweh sends Jeremiah to the potter’s house (1–4)
  2. Yahweh explains the potter’s work (5–10)
    1. Israel is clay in Yahweh’s hand (5–6)
    2. What Yahweh does to a nation depends on how that nation responds (7–10)
  3. Yahweh calls Judah to turn back, and the people refuse (11–12)
  4. Yahweh accuses Judah of forgetting him and announces that he will scatter them (13–17)
  5. Jeremiah’s opponents plot against him, and he prays against them (18–23)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in [18:14–17](../18/14.md) and [18:19–23](../18/19.md).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The potter’s house

A potter shaped vessels from clay on a pair of stone wheels that he turned by hand or foot. While the clay was still soft, he could press a spoiled vessel back into a lump and form it into something else. Yahweh uses this everyday scene as a picture of his freedom to deal with his people as he chooses.

### Yahweh relenting from what he has announced

In verses 7–10 Yahweh states that what he announces about a nation is not fixed. If a nation turns from its evil, he will not bring the disaster he spoke of; if a nation does evil, he will not bring the good he promised. This is the basis for his appeal to Judah in verse 11. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/repent]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations within quotations

In verse 11 Yahweh tells Jeremiah what to say to the people, and inside that instruction stands a message that begins “Thus says Yahweh” and continues in Yahweh’s own words, stacking three levels of quotation. If this would be confusing in your language, you may translate one or more levels as an indirect quotation.

### A prayer asking for harm to come on enemies

In verses 19–23 Jeremiah asks Yahweh to bring famine, sword, and bereavement on the men who plotted against him and not to forgive their sin. Translate these as requests that Jeremiah addresses to Yahweh, not as predictions of what will happen.

# Jeremiah 19 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh sends Jeremiah to buy a clay jar, carry it out to the valley where people have been sacrificing their children, and announce disaster there. Jeremiah then smashes the jar as a picture of what Yahweh will do to Jerusalem, and he repeats the message in the temple courtyard.

  1. Yahweh sends Jeremiah with a jar to the Valley of the Son of Hinnom (1–2)
  2. The message Jeremiah proclaims in the valley (3–9)
    1. Why Yahweh is bringing disaster on this place (3–5)
    2. The place will be renamed, and the people will be destroyed (6–9)
  3. Jeremiah breaks the jar and explains what it means (10–13)
  4. Jeremiah repeats the message in the courtyard of the temple (14–15)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Topheth and the Valley of the Son of Hinnom

This valley lay just outside Jerusalem, and Topheth was the site in it where the people burned their sons as offerings to Baal at the worship places they had built there. Yahweh announces that the valley will be renamed “the Valley of Slaughter,” since it will become the place where the people themselves are killed and buried. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/names/baal]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/highplaces]])

### The host of the heavens

Verse 13 refers to worship of the sun, moon, and stars, which the people carried out on the flat roofs of their houses by burning incense and pouring out drink offerings to gods other than Yahweh. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/incense]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/drinkoffering]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### The broken jar as a sign

Jeremiah does not only speak this message; he acts it out by smashing a jar that cannot be mended (verses 10–11). Translate this as something Jeremiah actually does, and keep the connection clear between the smashed jar and what Yahweh says he will do to the people and the city.

### Quotations within quotations

In verses 3–9 and again in verses 11–13, Yahweh tells Jeremiah what to say, Jeremiah is to address his hearers, and a messenger formula such as “Thus says Yahweh of Armies” introduces Yahweh’s own words, so that as many as four levels of quotation stand one inside another. If this would be confusing in your language, you may translate one or more levels as an indirect quotation.

# Jeremiah 20 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 20:7–18.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Pashhur

This chapter prophesied punishment against a specific leader named Pashhur. He was in charge of protecting the temple and had Jeremiah beaten and arrested. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/temple]])

### Jeremiah’s reaction

Jeremiah’s reaction contrasts with the reaction of the Jews in general. Although Jeremiah was not happy with Yahweh’s actions, he still trusted in Yahweh. On the other hand, the Jews were not happy with the prophecies Yahweh gave to Jeremiah, so they beat the prophet. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/trust]])

# Jeremiah 25 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 25:30–38.

Babylon will rule over Judah for seventy years. Because Yahweh is just, he will soon punish Babylon for their evil actions. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/justice]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/evil]])

# Jeremiah 30 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 3:5–24.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### God promises restoration

Despite the prophesied punishment in this chapter, Yahweh promises to restore Judah. In addition to this, he also declares that he will ultimately restore Israel. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet]], [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promise]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/restore]])

# Jeremiah 31 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 31:1–6, 8–22, 35–37.

The ULT sets [31:29](../31/29.md) farther to the right on the page than the rest of the text because it is an important quotation.

This chapter begins with a transition from the previous chapter. “At that time” is a reference to the day of restoration mentioned in [Jeremiah 30:24](../30/24.md). (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/restore]])

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The new covenant

This chapter is an important teaching regarding the new covenant. God will make a new covenant that will bring forgiveness of sins and a desire to obey God. Scholars disagree about whether this new covenant has begun. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/covenant]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/forgive]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sin]])

# Jeremiah 34 General Notes

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Law of Moses

According to the law of Moses, the people were required to free their indebted slaves after a period of time. The king led them in freeing their fellow Israelites whom they held as slaves, but later they changed their minds and enslaved them again. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/lawofmoses]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sin]])

Note: This refers to the fourth year of Jehoiakim’s reign. This can be stated clearly. Alternate translation: [in the fourth year of the reign of Jehoiakim]

Quote: Put the harness on the horses; mount up on the horses
Note: A “harness” is a set of straps placed on a horse so that it can pull a chariot. Here “mount up on the horses” means that the soldiers rode in the chariots that the horses were pulling.
A helmet is armor which protects the head in battle.
This phrase means to “sharpen” the spear.

The word “I” here refers to Yahweh. Yahweh uses a question to introduce the vision and to draw attention to what he says next. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation as in the UST.

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **terror**, you can express the same idea with a verbal form such as “terrified.” Alternate translation: [The Egyptian soldiers are terrified]

Quote: the swift cannot run away, and the soldiers cannot escape
Note: These two phrases share similar meanings and emphasize that no one, not even the strongest and fastest, can escape. Alternate translation: [even the swiftest soldier cannot escape]

Quote: They stumble in the north and fall beside the Euphrates River
Note: Both statements mean the same thing. Alternate translation: [The Egyptian soldiers suffer defeat and die in the north by the Euphrates River]

Quote: Who is this who rises like the Nile … the rivers?
Note: Yahweh uses a question to draw attention to what he is about to say concerning Egypt. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this question as a statement. Alternate translation: [Look at who rises like the Nile … the rivers.]

By **the streams**, Yahweh means the streams that branch off from the Nile River and would overflow at the time of year when the Nile River was at flood stage. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [like the streams of the Nile River at flood stage]

The Nile river floods its banks once a year, covering the surrounding area with water. Yahweh compares the kingdom of Egypt to the Nile because the Egyptian people think they are mighty enough to destroy cities in all the lands.

Quote: Egypt rises … Egypt says … I will
Note: Here “Egypt” represents all the people of Egypt. Alternate translation: [The Egyptians rise … The Egyptians say … We will]

Quote: Go up, horses. Be angry, you chariots
Note: Here “horses” and “chariots” represent the soldiers who use horses and chariots in battle. The leaders of Egypt are ordering their soldiers to start the battle. Alternate translation: [Go up to battle, you soldiers on horses. Fight furiously, you soldiers in chariots]

Quote: Let the soldiers go out, Cush and Put, men skillful with a shield
Note: This command can be addressed directly to the soldiers. What they were to go out for can be stated clearly. Alternate translation: [You soldiers from Cush and Put, who are skillful with your shields, go out to battle]
These are biblical names for the countries of Ethiopia and Libya.

Quote: Ludim, men skillful at bending their bows
Note: The ideas of soldiers and going out to battle are understood from earlier in the sentence. They can be repeated. This command can also be addressed directly to the soldiers. Alternate translation: [you soldiers from Lud, who are skillful at bending your bows, go out to battle]
This is the name of the people group from the nation of Lud. Lud is the biblical name for Lydia.

The phrase “bend the bow” means to pull the string of the bow back with an arrow in order to shoot the arrow. Alternate translation: [skillful at shooting arrows from their bows] or [skillful with the bow and arrow]

Quote: for the Lord Yahweh of hosts, and he will avenge himself on his foes
Note: Yahweh speaks of himself in third person. This can be stated in first person. Alternate translation: [for me, Lord Yahweh of hosts, and I will avenge myself on my foes]

Note: Both these phrases are saying similar thing and are combined to emphasize that there will be complete destruction. Alternate translation: [I will completely destroy my enemy. It will be like my sword devours them and gets drunk on their blood]

Note: Yahweh is speaking of **the sword** as if it were a living thing that could eat and **be satisfied** and drink and have its thirst **quenched**. Note: Yahweh avenging himself by causing the Egyptians to lose in battle against the Babylonians is spoken of as if the Egyptian army would be a sacrifice to Yahweh. Alternate translation: [For the Egyptians will be like a sacrifice]

Quote: Why are your mighty ones face-down on the ground? They will not stand
Note: Yahweh uses a question to mock the strength of the Egyptian soldiers. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this question as a statement. Alternate translation: [Your soldiers are face-down on the ground and will not stand]

Note: Alternate translation: [Yahweh causes more and more of your soldiers to stumble]

Quote: Pack for yourselves baggage to carry into exile
Note: Alternate translation: [Prepare to go into exile]

Yahweh is repeating the word **beautiful** and the word **coming** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that that they convey. Note: This speaks of a day as if it travels and arrives in a location. Alternate translation: [they will experience disaster on that day]

Note: The enemies coming with the weapons to destroy the Egyptians is spoken of as if they were woodcutters with axes preparing to cut down a tree.

Note: This continues speaking of the enemy army attacking the Egyptians as if the army were woodcutters cutting down trees. Alternate translation: [The enemy army will kill many Egyptians like woodcutters cutting down a forest … even though there are very many trees]

Note: The people of Egypt are spoken of as if they were the daughter of Egypt. Alternate translation: [The enemy army will humiliate the people of Egypt]

Note: Here “hand” represents power or control. Alternate translation: [I, Yahweh, will allow the people from the north to defeat the Egyptians]

Here “Egypt” represents the people. Alternate translation: [all the people of Egypt and the gods they worship]

Note: Here “hand” represents power or control. Alternate translation: [I will allow those who are wanting to kill them to defeat them]

Note: Here “hand” represents power or control. “Nebuchadnezzar … his servants” names specifically “the ones seeking their lives.” Alternate translation: [that is, I will allow Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and his servants to defeat the Egyptians]

Quote: Then after this Egypt will be inhabited
Note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Then after this, people will live in Egypt again]

Quote: my servant Jacob, do not fear. Do not be dismayed, Israel
Note: These two phrases mean the same thing. Alternate translation: [people of Israel, my servants, do not be afraid]

Quote: from the land of their captivity
Note: Alternate translation: [from the land where they are captives]

Note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **destruction**, you can express the same idea with the verb “destroy.” Alternate translation: [I will completely destroy all the nations]

Quote: will certainly not leave you unpunished
Note: This can be stated in positive form. Alternate translation: [will certainly punish you]

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Flood waters

This chapter uses the imagery of a flood to describe the enemies who conquer the Philistines. Their destruction will be swift and complete. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

Quote: This is the word of Yahweh that came to Jeremiah
Note: The idiom “the word of Yahweh that came to” is used to introduce a special message from God. See how you translated this in [Jeremiah 14:1](../14/01.md), and make any changes as needed. Alternate translation: [This is the message that Yahweh gave to Jeremiah]
The idiom “this word came to” is used to introduce a special message from God. Alternate translation: [Yahweh gave this message to Jeremiah] or [Yahweh spoke this message to Jeremiah]
Here “Pharaoh” represents the Egyptians army. Alternate translation: [before Pharaoh’s army]
The word “see” alerts us to pay attention to what is about to be said.

Quote: floods of water are rising in the north. They will be like an overflowing river!
Note: The two phrases have a similar meaning. Alternate translation: [an army in the north will come like a flood. They will be powerful like an overflowing river]
This continues speaking of the army from the north as an overflowing river. Alternate translation: [like an overflowing river, the army from the north will destroy the land]

Quote: At the sound of the stamping of their strong horses’ hooves, at the roar of their chariots and the noise of their wheels
Note: Together these represent the sounds of an oncoming army.

Quote: at the roar of their chariots and the noise of their wheels
Note: These two phrase have similar meanings and they are combined to emphasize the loud noise they will make. Alternate translation: [at the very loud sound of the wheels of the chariots]

Quote: For the day is coming that will devastate all of the Philistines, to cut off from Tyre
Note: This speaks of a day as if it were something that travels and arrives in a place. Alternate translation: [For on that day, the enemy army will devastate all of the Philistines and cut off from Tyre]

Quote: to cut off from Tyre and Sidon every survivor who wants to help them
Note: Removing someone is spoken of as if they were cut off the way a person may cut a branch from a tree or a piece of cloth from a garment. Alternate translation: [to remove anyone who may want to help Tyre and Sidon]
This is the name of an island of the northern region of the Philistines.

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **baldness**, you can express the same idea with a verbal form such as “bald.” Alternate translation: [The people of Gaza will shave their heads bald]
The shaving of the entire head or portions of the head is a sign of great sorrow practiced by idol worshipers in nations such as Philistia.

Quote: the people … will be made silent
Note: This could mean: (1) the people will be silent because they are mourning or (2) this is a euphemism that means the enemy soldiers will kill them.

Quote: How long will you cut yourself in mourning?
Note: Yahweh uses a question to emphasize that the people of Ashkelon will never stop mourning. Alternate translation: [You will forever cut yourselves in mourning.]

Shaving one’s head and cutting one’s body was a symbolic action by which person in that culture showed that they were mourning for someone who had died. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation, as in the UST, or in a footnote.

Quote: sword of Yahweh! How long will it be until you become silent? Go back to your scabbard! Stop and be silent.
Note: The Philistines speak to the sword of Yahweh as if it were a person who could hear them. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, you who are holding your sword! When will you stop striking us with your sword? Stop your sword and put it back in its scabbard!]
Yahweh punishing the Philistines by sending the army from the north is spoken of as if Yahweh were striking them with a sword.

Quote: How long will it be until you become silent?
Note: The people of the Philistines use this question to express their deep frustration about the devastation caused by their enemies. This may be translated as a statement. Alternate translation: [Please be silent!] or [Please, Yahweh, stop striking us with your sword!]
A sword makes a noise as it slashes back and forth. Asking the sword to be silent means to ask it to stop slashing and killing. Alternate translation: [you rest] or [you stop slashing]
This is the case used to protect the blade of a sword.

Quote: How can it rest … along the sea?
Note: Here Jeremiah is speaking. He continues speaking of the sword of Yahweh as if it were a person who could rest. Yahweh punishing the Philistines by sending the army of the north is spoken of as if Yahweh were striking the people with a sword. Alternate translation: [It cannot rest … along the sea.]

Quote: How can it rest when Yahweh has commanded it, when he has ordered … the sea?
Note: Jeremiah uses a question to mean that the sword cannot stop since Yahweh has commanded it to continue killing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this question as a statement. Alternate translation: [It cannot stop, for Yahweh has commanded it. He has ordered … the sea.]

# Jeremiah 49 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

The ULT sets the lines in 49:1–11, 14–27, 29–33, 37–39 farther to the right on the page than the rest of the text because they are part of a long quotation.

Jeremiah’s prophesies about other nations conclude in this chapter. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet]])

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Covenant with Abraham

Ammon is destroyed because it drove the people of the tribe of Gad from their homeland. This is in line with the promises of the covenant Yahweh made with Abraham to curse those who curse Abraham’s descendants. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promise]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/covenant]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/curse]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

# Jeremiah 50 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 50:1–5, 6–46.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Babylon destroyed

Babylon will be conquered and the Jews will return to their homeland. At this time, Babylon controlled almost the entire Near East. The fulfillment of this prophecy would have been unthinkable. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/fulfill]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet]])
